## Overview

Concentration-QTc (C-QTc) modeling is a standard pharmacometric approach
in cardiac safety assessment. Under the ICH E14/S7B Q&As (R1, 2026),
C-QTc modeling can serve as an alternative to the by-time-point
intersection-union test (IUT) for evaluating a drug's potential to prolong
the QTc interval. The two approaches test different hypotheses: the IUT
asks whether ΔΔQTc exceeds 10 ms at any scheduled time point; C-QTc asks
whether ΔΔQTc exceeds 10 ms at a clinically relevant concentration.

This scenario walks through a concentration-ΔΔQTcF analysis using an
open-source ECG dataset. We demonstrate how to:

1. Prepare ECG and concentration data, including **placebo correction**
2. Run the **exploratory checks** required by ICH E14 Q&A 5.1
3. Fit the **prespecified linear** mixed-effects C-QTc model
4. Compute the **regulatory prediction** (ΔΔQTcF with 90% CI at geometric-mean Cmax)
5. Fit a **nonlinear Emax** model on a drug where the relationship saturates
6. Summarize **categorical outliers**

The dataset comes from PhysioNet
([Johannesen et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1038/clpt.2014.155);
[doi:10.13026/C2HP45](https://doi.org/10.13026/C2HP45)), a five-way
crossover ECG study in 22 healthy volunteers receiving dofetilide,
quinidine, ranolazine, verapamil, and placebo. This study was designed to
evaluate multichannel block effects on ECG morphology; we use it here as
a teaching dataset for the C-QTc workflow.

**Scope and limitations.** A C-QTc upper bound below 10 ms is a claim at
the exposure covered by the data. These single-dose data do not cover
steady state, supratherapeutic exposure, or drug interactions. A real
regulatory assessment would require exposure at approximately 2x the high
clinical exposure, or the nonclinical "double negative" (E14/S7B Q&A R1,
5.1), together with a prespecified analysis plan and BLQ handling rule.
Dofetilide is a selective hERG blocker with a large, well-known QTc
effect (~70 ms at therapeutic Cmax), so the 10 ms decision criterion is
here a teaching device rather than a verdict.

---

## Data preparation

### Download and inspect the raw data

Each row is a single ECG replicate; there are three replicates per time
point per subject per treatment period.

```{r download, eval = FALSE}
url <- "https://physionet.org/physiobank/database/ecgrdvq/SCR-002.Clinical.Data.csv"
raw <- read.csv(url)
```

### Compute QTcF and ΔΔQTcF

The Fridericia correction adjusts QT for heart rate:
QTcF = QT / (RR / 1000)^(1/3), where RR is in milliseconds.

The change-from-baseline ΔQTcF is computed per subject and treatment
period. The placebo-corrected ΔΔQTcF is then obtained by subtracting the
time-matched placebo ΔQTcF for each subject (valid in a crossover design;
Garnett 2018, Table 4).

```{r prep, eval = FALSE}
# Fridericia correction
raw$QTcF <- raw$QT / (raw$RR / 1000)^(1/3)

# Average triplicate ECGs at each time point.
# Note: EXDOSE is intentionally excluded from the grouping formula
# so that placebo records (where EXDOSE is NA) are retained.
agg <- aggregate(
  cbind(QTcF, PCSTRESN, RR) ~ RANDID + EXTRT + TPT + BASELINE +
    SEX + AGE + WGHT,
  data = raw,
  FUN = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  na.action = na.pass
)

# Per-subject, per-period baseline QTcF
baselines <- agg[agg$BASELINE == "Y",]
bl_avg <- aggregate(QTcF ~ RANDID + EXTRT, data = baselines, FUN = mean)
names(bl_avg)[3] <- "BL_QTcF"

# Merge baseline and compute delta QTcF
agg <- merge(agg, bl_avg, by = c("RANDID", "EXTRT"))
agg$dQTcF <- agg$QTcF - agg$BL_QTcF

# Placebo correction: subtract time-matched placebo dQTcF per subject
placebo <- agg[agg$EXTRT == "Placebo" & agg$BASELINE == "N",
               c("RANDID", "TPT", "dQTcF")]
names(placebo)[3] <- "dQTcF_placebo"

active <- agg[agg$EXTRT != "Placebo" & agg$BASELINE == "N" &
              !is.na(agg$PCSTRESN),]
active <- merge(active, placebo, by = c("RANDID", "TPT"), all.x = TRUE)
active$ddQTcF <- active$dQTcF - active$dQTcF_placebo
```

### Prepare the dofetilide modeling dataset

We focus on dofetilide, a selective hERG channel blocker with a large,
well-characterized QTc effect. Only post-dose records with measured
plasma concentration are retained.

```{r filter, eval = FALSE}
dof <- active[active$EXTRT == "Dofetilide",]

# Concentration is in pg/mL; convert to ng/mL
dof$CONC <- dof$PCSTRESN / 1000

# Centered baseline QTcF (for the model's baseline covariate)
mean_bl <- mean(dof$BL_QTcF)
dof$BLc <- dof$BL_QTcF - mean_bl

# Format for ferx
ferx_data <- data.frame(
  ID   = as.integer(factor(dof$RANDID)),
  TIME = dof$TPT,
  DV   = round(dof$ddQTcF, 4),
  MDV  = 0,
  CONC = round(dof$CONC, 4),
  BLc  = round(dof$BLc, 4),
  SEX  = ifelse(dof$SEX == "F", 1, 0)
)
ferx_data <- ferx_data[order(ferx_data$ID, ferx_data$TIME),]
write.csv(ferx_data, "dofetilide_ddqtcf.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Geometric mean Cmax
cmax_per_subj <- tapply(dof$CONC, dof$RANDID, max)
gm_cmax <- exp(mean(log(cmax_per_subj)))

head(ferx_data, 6)
#>   ID TIME      DV MDV   CONC      BLc SEX
#> 1  1  0.5  4.3706   0 0.1200 -13.3733   1
#> 2  1  1.0 18.9475   0 1.6100 -13.3733   1
#> 3  1  1.5 63.4094   0 1.9300 -13.3733   1
#> 4  1  2.0 68.1426   0 2.4300 -13.3733   1
#> 5  1  2.5 66.6889   0 2.9000 -13.3733   1
#> 6  1  3.0 72.4598   0 2.9400 -13.3733   1

cat("Geometric mean Cmax:", round(gm_cmax, 2), "ng/mL\n")
#> Geometric mean Cmax: 2.71 ng/mL
```

---

## Exploratory checks

Before fitting a C-QTc model, the ICH E14 Q&As and the Garnett 2018
white paper require several exploratory assessments.

### Heart-rate change

If mean ΔΔHR exceeds approximately 10 bpm, the QTcF correction may be
inadequate and an alternative correction should be considered.

```{r explore-hr, eval = FALSE}
# Compute mean delta-delta HR by drug and time
raw$HR <- 60000 / raw$RR
agg_hr <- aggregate(HR ~ RANDID + EXTRT + TPT + BASELINE,
                    data = raw, FUN = mean)
bl_hr <- agg_hr[agg_hr$BASELINE == "Y",]
bl_hr_avg <- aggregate(HR ~ RANDID + EXTRT, data = bl_hr, FUN = mean)
names(bl_hr_avg)[3] <- "BL_HR"
agg_hr <- merge(agg_hr, bl_hr_avg, by = c("RANDID", "EXTRT"))
agg_hr$dHR <- agg_hr$HR - agg_hr$BL_HR

plac_hr <- agg_hr[agg_hr$EXTRT == "Placebo" & agg_hr$BASELINE == "N",
                  c("RANDID", "TPT", "dHR")]
names(plac_hr)[3] <- "dHR_placebo"
active_hr <- agg_hr[agg_hr$EXTRT != "Placebo" & agg_hr$BASELINE == "N",]
active_hr <- merge(active_hr, plac_hr, by = c("RANDID", "TPT"))
active_hr$ddHR <- active_hr$dHR - active_hr$dHR_placebo

# Mean ddHR by drug and time
ddhr_means <- aggregate(ddHR ~ EXTRT + TPT, data = active_hr, FUN = mean)
for (drug in unique(ddhr_means$EXTRT)) {
  mx <- max(ddhr_means$ddHR[ddhr_means$EXTRT == drug])
  cat(drug, "max mean ddHR:", round(mx, 1), "bpm\n")
}
#> Dofetilide max mean ddHR: 2.2 bpm
#> Quinidine Sulph max mean ddHR: 9.7 bpm
#> Verapamil HCL max mean ddHR: 9.4 bpm
#> Ranolazine max mean ddHR: 7.6 bpm
```

For dofetilide, the heart-rate effect is small (2.2 bpm), so QTcF is
adequate. Quinidine and verapamil approach the 10 bpm concern level;
sensitivity analyses with an alternative correction (e.g., population
QTcP) would be appropriate for those drugs.

### Concentration-ΔΔQTcF scatter and linearity

A decile plot helps assess whether the relationship is approximately
linear or shows saturation.

```{r explore-scatter, eval = FALSE}
# Decile plot for dofetilide
deciles <- cut(ferx_data$CONC,
               breaks = quantile(ferx_data$CONC, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.1)),
               include.lowest = TRUE)
decile_means <- tapply(ferx_data$DV, deciles, mean)
decile_conc  <- tapply(ferx_data$CONC, deciles, mean)

plot(ferx_data$CONC, ferx_data$DV,
     xlab = "Dofetilide concentration (ng/mL)",
     ylab = expression(paste(Delta, Delta, "QTcF (ms)")),
     pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3))
points(decile_conc, decile_means, pch = 18, cex = 2, col = "darkred")
abline(h = c(0, 10), lty = c(2, 3), col = c("grey50", "red"))
legend("topleft", pch = 18, col = "darkred", legend = "Decile means")
```

For dofetilide, the decile means rise approximately linearly from about
4 ms to 74 ms across the concentration range. This supports a linear
model. For quinidine, the decile means flatten at higher concentrations,
motivating an Emax model (see below).

### Hysteresis

Concentration-effect hysteresis (clockwise or counterclockwise loops in a
concentration-vs-effect plot over time) can indicate delayed drug effect
or active metabolites. A formal hysteresis assessment would use an effect
compartment; here we show the exploratory loop plot.

```{r explore-hysteresis, eval = FALSE}
# Mean concentration and ddQTcF by time for dofetilide
time_means <- aggregate(cbind(CONC, DV) ~ TIME, data = ferx_data, FUN = mean)
plot(time_means$CONC, time_means$DV, type = "b", pch = 16,
     xlab = "Mean concentration (ng/mL)",
     ylab = expression(paste("Mean ", Delta, Delta, "QTcF (ms)")),
     main = "Hysteresis loop: Dofetilide")
text(time_means$CONC, time_means$DV, labels = paste0(time_means$TIME, "h"),
     pos = 3, cex = 0.7)
```

---

## Linear C-QTc model

### Model specification

The model follows the structure recommended by Garnett 2018, adapted for
a placebo-corrected crossover analysis. Because ΔΔQTcF already accounts
for treatment and time effects through placebo subtraction, the model
does not require explicit TRT or categorical TIME terms:

    ΔΔQTcF_ij = (intercept + θ_BL * BLc_i + η_int,i) + (slope + η_slope,i) * CONC_ij + ε_ij

The model includes IIV on both the intercept and the slope (Garnett 2018,
Eq. 1). The centered baseline QTcF covariate (`BLc = QTcF_baseline -
mean`) accounts for between-subject differences in baseline
repolarization.

```{r linear-model-write, eval = FALSE}
writeLines("
[parameters]
  theta TVINTERCEPT(0.0, -50.0, 50.0)
  theta TVSLOPE(20.0, -50.0, 100.0)
  theta TBL(0.0, -2.0, 2.0)

  omega ETA_INTERCEPT ~ 100.0 (variance)
  omega ETA_SLOPE ~ 10.0 (variance)

  sigma ADD ~ 100.0 (variance)

[individual_parameters]
  INTERCEPT = TVINTERCEPT + TBL * BLc + ETA_INTERCEPT
  SLOPE = TVSLOPE + ETA_SLOPE

[structural_model]
  y = INTERCEPT + SLOPE * CONC

[covariates]
  CONC continuous
  BLc  continuous

[error_model]
  DV ~ additive(ADD)

[fit_options]
  method     = focei
  covariance = true
", "qtc_linear.ferx")
```

This is a **compartment-free** model (no ODEs, no dosing events). The
prediction equation defines the model directly, analogous to NONMEM
`$PRED`. Drug concentration enters via the `[covariates]` block.

### Fit the model

```{r linear-fit, eval = FALSE}
library(ferx)

fit_linear <- ferx_fit(model = "qtc_linear.ferx", data = "dofetilide_ddqtcf.csv")
fit_linear
#> Model: qtc_linear  |  Method: FOCEI  |  Subjects: 22  |  Obs: 328
#> STATUS: CONVERGED   35 iterations   0.0s
#> OFV: 2028.7943    AIC: 2040.7943
#>
#> THETA
#> Parameter            Estimate           SE       %RSE
#> TVINTERCEPT         -3.812723     1.962962       51.5
#> TVSLOPE             28.588674     1.468448        5.1
#> TBL                  0.057602     0.111940      194.3
#>
#> OMEGA
#>   ETA_INTERCEPT  [additive]  = 35.46  (SD = 5.96)   SE = 21.56
#>   ETA_SLOPE      [additive]  = 30.71  (SD = 5.54)   SE = 12.12
#>
#> SIGMA
#>   ADD  [additive]  = 12.07  (SD = 12.07, var = 145.74)  SE = 0.50
```

With placebo correction, the intercept is -3.8 ms (SE 2.0), close to
zero as expected. The centered baseline covariate (TBL) is not
significant here (RSE 194%), consistent with the white paper's
observation that covariate analysis is not routinely informative in
healthy-volunteer studies. The slope of 28.6 ms per ng/mL is precisely
estimated (%RSE 5.1%).

### Regulatory prediction

The regulatory deliverable is the predicted ΔΔQTcF at the geometric-mean
Cmax with a two-sided 90% confidence interval, computed by the delta
method. The geometric-mean Cmax is treated as fixed (Garnett 2018,
Eqs. 3-5).

```{r linear-predict, eval = FALSE}
# Extract estimates
ests <- fit_linear$estimates
int_est   <- ests$estimate[ests$param == "TVINTERCEPT"]
slope_est <- ests$estimate[ests$param == "TVSLOPE"]

# Predicted ddQTcF at geometric-mean Cmax
ddqtc_pred <- int_est + slope_est * gm_cmax

# Delta-method SE: var(int + slope*C) = var(int) + C^2*var(slope) + 2*C*cov(int,slope)
cov_mat <- fit_linear$cov_matrix
idx_int   <- which(rownames(cov_mat) == "TVINTERCEPT")
idx_slope <- which(rownames(cov_mat) == "TVSLOPE")

var_pred <- cov_mat[idx_int, idx_int] +
  gm_cmax^2 * cov_mat[idx_slope, idx_slope] +
  2 * gm_cmax * cov_mat[idx_int, idx_slope]
se_pred <- sqrt(var_pred)

# Two-sided 90% CI
z90 <- qnorm(0.95)
ci_lo <- ddqtc_pred - z90 * se_pred
ci_hi <- ddqtc_pred + z90 * se_pred

cat("Geometric mean Cmax:", round(gm_cmax, 2), "ng/mL\n")
cat("Predicted ddQTcF:", round(ddqtc_pred, 1), "ms\n")
cat("90% CI:", round(ci_lo, 1), "to", round(ci_hi, 1), "ms\n")
#> Geometric mean Cmax: 2.71 ng/mL
#> Predicted ddQTcF: 73.7 ms
#> 90% CI: 67.6 to 79.7 ms
```

The upper bound of 79.7 ms is far above the 10 ms threshold, as expected
for a potent hERG blocker. This confirms dofetilide's known QTc liability
and demonstrates the analysis workflow.

---

## Nonlinear Emax model (quinidine)

Nonlinear models should be considered when the exploratory linearity
(decile) plot shows saturation. For dofetilide over 0.04-3.3 ng/mL, the
relationship is approximately linear and an Emax model is not
identifiable (TVEMAX hits its upper bound).

Quinidine is a better candidate: its decile means flatten at higher
concentrations. We fit an Emax model with an E0 intercept term:

    ΔΔQTcF_ij = (E0 + η_E0,i) + Emax_i * CONC_ij / (EC50 + CONC_ij) + ε_ij

```{r emax-quinidine, eval = FALSE}
# Prepare quinidine data
quin <- active[active$EXTRT == "Quinidine Sulph",]
quin$CONC <- quin$PCSTRESN / 1000  # ng/mL to ug/mL
mean_bl_q <- mean(quin$BL_QTcF)
quin$BLc <- quin$BL_QTcF - mean_bl_q

quin_data <- data.frame(
  ID   = as.integer(factor(quin$RANDID)),
  TIME = quin$TPT,
  DV   = round(quin$ddQTcF, 4),
  MDV  = 0,
  CONC = round(quin$CONC, 4),
  BLc  = round(quin$BLc, 4)
)
quin_data <- quin_data[order(quin_data$ID, quin_data$TIME),]
write.csv(quin_data, "quinidine_ddqtcf.csv", row.names = FALSE)

writeLines("
[parameters]
  theta TVE0(0.0, -50.0, 50.0)
  theta TVEMAX(80.0, 1.0, 300.0)
  theta TVEC50(1.0, 0.01, 20.0)

  omega ETA_E0 ~ 100.0 (variance)
  omega ETA_EMAX ~ 0.09

  sigma ADD ~ 100.0 (variance)

[individual_parameters]
  E0   = TVE0 + ETA_E0
  EMAX = TVEMAX * exp(ETA_EMAX)
  EC50 = TVEC50

[structural_model]
  y = E0 + EMAX * CONC / (EC50 + CONC)

[covariates]
  CONC continuous

[error_model]
  DV ~ additive(ADD)

[fit_options]
  method     = focei
  covariance = true
", "qtc_emax.ferx")

fit_emax <- ferx_fit(model = "qtc_emax.ferx", data = "quinidine_ddqtcf.csv")
fit_emax
```

An Emax model that estimates well on these data indicates saturation at
higher quinidine concentrations. For nonlinear models, the delta-method
CI may be replaced by a bootstrap CI for more robust inference.

---

## Verapamil: a small-effect case

Verapamil combines hERG-channel and calcium-channel blocking, producing
a small net QTc effect. This makes it useful for demonstrating the
analysis when the upper bound is near the 10 ms threshold.

```{r verapamil, eval = FALSE}
ver <- active[active$EXTRT == "Verapamil HCL",]
ver$CONC <- ver$PCSTRESN  # already in ng/mL
mean_bl_v <- mean(ver$BL_QTcF)
ver$BLc <- ver$BL_QTcF - mean_bl_v

ver_data <- data.frame(
  ID = as.integer(factor(ver$RANDID)), TIME = ver$TPT,
  DV = round(ver$ddQTcF, 4), MDV = 0,
  CONC = round(ver$CONC, 4), BLc = round(ver$BLc, 4)
)
ver_data <- ver_data[order(ver_data$ID, ver_data$TIME),]
write.csv(ver_data, "verapamil_ddqtcf.csv", row.names = FALSE)

fit_ver <- ferx_fit(model = "qtc_linear.ferx", data = "verapamil_ddqtcf.csv")

# Prediction at GM Cmax
cmax_v <- exp(mean(log(tapply(ver$CONC, ver$RANDID, max))))
ests_v <- fit_ver$estimates
int_v <- ests_v$estimate[ests_v$param == "TVINTERCEPT"]
slope_v <- ests_v$estimate[ests_v$param == "TVSLOPE"]
ddqtc_v <- int_v + slope_v * cmax_v

cov_v <- fit_ver$cov_matrix
idx_i <- which(rownames(cov_v) == "TVINTERCEPT")
idx_s <- which(rownames(cov_v) == "TVSLOPE")
var_v <- cov_v[idx_i,idx_i] + cmax_v^2 * cov_v[idx_s,idx_s] +
  2 * cmax_v * cov_v[idx_i,idx_s]
se_v <- sqrt(var_v)
ci_hi_v <- ddqtc_v + qnorm(0.95) * se_v

cat("Verapamil GM Cmax:", round(cmax_v, 1), "ng/mL\n")
cat("ddQTcF:", round(ddqtc_v, 1), "ms, 90% CI:",
    round(ddqtc_v - qnorm(0.95)*se_v, 1), "to", round(ci_hi_v, 1), "ms\n")
cat("Upper bound < 10 ms:", ci_hi_v < 10, "\n")
#> Verapamil GM Cmax: 113.6 ng/mL
#> ddQTcF: 3.6 ms, 90% CI: 0.0 to 7.2 ms
#> Upper bound < 10 ms: TRUE
```

The upper bound of 7.2 ms is below 10 ms at this single 120 mg dose's
Cmax. Note that this does not constitute a full negative QT assessment:
the verapamil label allows up to 480 mg/day, and these data cover only a
single 120 mg dose. A complete assessment would require exposure coverage
at the high clinical exposure.

---

## Categorical outlier analysis

ICH E14 (Section 3.2.2) requires a categorical analysis alongside the
central-tendency model. This tabulates the number of subject-time-point
observations exceeding absolute QTcF thresholds and change-from-baseline
thresholds.

```{r outliers, eval = FALSE}
# Categorical outliers by arm (counts of subject-time-point observations)
for (drug in c("Dofetilide", "Quinidine Sulph", "Verapamil HCL",
               "Ranolazine", "Placebo")) {
  sub <- agg[agg$EXTRT == drug & agg$BASELINE == "N",]
  cat(sprintf("%-18s QTcF>450: %3d  >480: %3d  >500: %3d  dQTcF>30: %3d  >60: %3d\n",
      drug,
      sum(sub$QTcF > 450, na.rm = TRUE),
      sum(sub$QTcF > 480, na.rm = TRUE),
      sum(sub$QTcF > 500, na.rm = TRUE),
      sum(sub$dQTcF > 30, na.rm = TRUE),
      sum(sub$dQTcF > 60, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
#> Dofetilide         QTcF>450:  78  >480:  26  >500:   8  dQTcF>30: 172  >60:  55
#> Quinidine Sulph    QTcF>450: 106  >480:  50  >500:  22  dQTcF>30: 202  >60:  85
#> Verapamil HCL      QTcF>450:   0  >480:   0  >500:   0  dQTcF>30:   0  >60:   0
#> Ranolazine         QTcF>450:   1  >480:   0  >500:   0  dQTcF>30:   3  >60:   0
#> Placebo            QTcF>450:   0  >480:   0  >500:   0  dQTcF>30:   0  >60:   0
```

Dofetilide and quinidine show numerous observations above all thresholds,
consistent with their known QTc liability. Verapamil, ranolazine, and
placebo show none or very few.

---

## Diagnostics

After selecting the best model, standard NLME diagnostics apply.

```{r diagnostics, eval = FALSE}
# Diagnostic plots
plot(fit_linear)

# Conditional weighted residuals vs population prediction
sdtab <- fit_linear$sdtab
plot(sdtab$PRED, sdtab$CWRES,
     xlab = "Population prediction (ms)", ylab = "CWRES",
     main = "CWRES vs PRED")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Individual predictions vs observed
plot(sdtab$DV, sdtab$IPRED,
     xlab = expression(paste("Observed ", Delta, Delta, "QTcF (ms)")),
     ylab = "Individual prediction (ms)",
     main = "IPRED vs DV")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
```

---

## Summary

| Model | Parameters | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | intercept, slope, baseline, omega(2), sigma | Standard ICH E14 analysis; prespecified primary model |
| Emax | E0, Emax, EC50, omega(2), sigma | Saturating drugs (when decile plot shows nonlinearity) |

Both models are **compartment-free** in ferx, meaning they use no ODEs
and no dose records. Drug concentration enters the model directly from
the data via the `[covariates]` block.

**Key analysis requirements** for a regulatory C-QTc submission:

- **Endpoint:** ΔΔQTcF (placebo-corrected, Fridericia-corrected)
- **Prespecification:** model, selection criteria, and BLQ rule
- **Exploratory checks:** heart rate, QT correction adequacy, hysteresis,
  linearity
- **Prediction:** at geometric-mean Cmax with a delta-method 90% CI
  (including the covariance term)
- **Exposure coverage:** approximately 2x the high clinical exposure, or
  the nonclinical double negative
- **Categorical outliers:** QTcF > 450/480/500 ms and ΔQTcF > 30/60 ms
